title: Precious Time
author: Kurt Wootton
summary: Kurt Wootton compares the start of a school year to the blank page, canvas, or empty stage that artists face, a mix of intimidation and possibility. Quoting Mary Oliver's question about what we plan to do with our one wild and precious life, he argues that teachers hold a precious power to decide what the class will do with its time together. That means tuning out the noise of mandates, packaged curricula, and fads while still preparing students for their next steps. Content matters, he says, but it is not the whole journey, and the first question in the room should be what extraordinary work the group will do together. He illustrates with a story of opening a middle school's year, acknowledging that teachers would rather be prepping and promising them a day worth being there. The post closes with a modest, humane aim: bring a little magic each day so students leave feeling taller and inspired.
points: Students arrive as full people with their own talents, passions, hopes, and fears, so the classroom is never a blank page.
Teachers have the power to decide how a class spends its shared time and should filter out the white noise of mandates, packaged curricula, and fads.
Content is necessary for excellent work but is not the whole journey; the opening question can be what extraordinary work we will do together.
Naming the audience's honest reluctance, as he did with teachers who would rather be prepping, builds credibility before asking for their attention.
The realistic goal is not an extraordinary experience every day but daily effort to bring a little magic so people feel the time was well spent.
quotes: We have a precious power as a teacher—we have the ability to decide what we will collectively do with our time together.
We must tune out the white noise—a cacophony of standards, district mandates, packaged curricula, the latest educational theories and fads.
Content is important. It is absolutely necessary for creating exceptional work, but it isn’t the entire journey.
Our students arrive with full and robust lives. They bring their own talents, passions, interests, hopes, and fears.
At the end of the day, my goal is for you to feel that there was nowhere better you could have spent your workday than right here, together in this room.
But that doesn’t mean that we can’t try every day to bring a little magic to our experiences together.
I hope when someone leaves my classroom they feel a little bit taller. I hope they feel inspired, and I hope they feel like the time we spent together was well worth it—perhaps even precious.
